316.title: Peace with God (Romans 5:1–11)
316.hook: suffering, patience, character, hope; while we were still sinners, Christ died
316.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to Romans 5:1–5 in times of illness or loss, and it's often read at funerals and in hospital chaplaincy, where people look back together on what a hard season grew.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was faith, pistis, trust: an old man under the stars, and your line was counted as right. Did you open your hand on the thing you were gripping? Day three hundred sixteen.

Ask someone you admire how they got that way, the steady one, the one people call at two in the morning. Almost nobody says: everything went well for me. They say: the year my dad was sick. The job I lost. The long winter after the divorce. Something hard happened, and something grew in the hard ground. Nobody would choose it. Hardly anyone would give back what grew. Paul knew this pattern from the inside. He'd been shipwrecked, beaten, jailed, and he was still writing letters. In Romans chapter five he traces the pattern step by step, and he starts it somewhere surprising: with peace.
screen: `HOW DID THEY GET THAT WAY?` → `SOMETHING HARD HAPPENED.` → `PAUL STARTS WITH PEACE.`

segments.voice: Chapter five opens, in the King James Bible: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." The Greek word for peace is eirene, and behind it stands the Hebrew shalom: not just no fighting, but wholeness, everything in its right place. After four chapters about guilt and grace, this is where Paul lands. The war is over. Then he does something odd. He says we glory, we even boast, in tribulations. Not because suffering is good. Because of what can grow in it. Listen to the chain: "tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed." Four links. Hard times grow endurance. Endurance grows what the King James calls experience; the Greek means tested character, like metal that's been through the fire and proved true. And that tested character grows hope. And hope, Paul says, doesn't let you down. Maketh not ashamed: an echo of Paul's opening a few days ago, not ashamed. Why doesn't it disappoint? Because, he says, the love of God has been poured into our hearts. Then comes the line that holds the whole chapter up: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Not after we got better. While. Paul points out that people will rarely die even for a good person. This love didn't wait for anyone to deserve it. Christians hear this passage very differently in hard times and easy ones, and many say it's only in hindsight that they can see the chain at all.
screen: `EIRENE: SHALOM, WHOLENESS.` · `GLORY IN TRIBULATIONS.` · `PATIENCE, TESTED CHARACTER, HOPE.` · `WHILE WE WERE YET SINNERS.` · then, large: `HOPE MAKETH NOT ASHAMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list one hardship that grew you. Settle, and breathe. Go back through your life slowly and find one hard season that, looking back, grew something in you. Patience. Compassion. Honesty. A friend you'd never have met. Don't pretend it was good; it may still hurt. Just name the hardship, and then name what grew. If a hardship you're in right now comes to mind instead, let it be there too, without forcing any lesson on it yet. If you pray, you can give thanks for what grew, and ask for hope in what hasn't yet. The bell holds the time.
Peace with God. Eirene in Greek, shalom in Hebrew: wholeness, the war over, everything in its right place.
Your line: hope does not disappoint. Today, tell one person about a hard season that grew something in you, or ask them about theirs. Day three hundred sixteen.

317.title: Adam and Christ (Romans 5:12–21)
317.hook: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more
317.howItsDone: Christians read Romans 5 when they teach about sin and salvation, and in the Easter Vigil's ancient hymn, the Exsultet, many churches sing of Adam's fall and of the grace that came after it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peace with God, and the chain from tribulation to hope. Your line was hope does not disappoint. Did you tell someone about a hard season that grew you? Day three hundred seventeen.

Some things you inherit without asking. Your grandmother's nose. Your family's way of going quiet when things get tense. A house, or a debt. You didn't choose any of it, and it shapes you anyway. Paul, in the second half of Romans chapter five, steps way back from Rome and from his own day, all the way back to the garden in Genesis. He's thinking about the whole human family and what it has inherited. And he sets two figures side by side, like two ends of a seesaw: the first man, and one more. Today is those two names.
screen: `THINGS YOU INHERIT WITHOUT ASKING.` → `BACK TO THE GARDEN.` → `TWO FIGURES, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Paul begins, in the King James Bible: "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned." One man, Adam, opened a door, and sin and death came through it into the whole human story. Then Paul sets up the other end of the seesaw: "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." Adam and Christ. One disobeyed, one obeyed. One brought death, one brings life. But here's what Paul keeps insisting: it isn't an even seesaw. Again and again he says much more. The gift is not like the fall. Then comes the line of the day: "But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound." Paul is so eager here he reaches for a rare super-word in Greek: grace super-abounded, over-overflowed. However big the mess gets, grace is bigger. Now, Christians understand the Adam side differently, so here's who says what. In the West, following Augustine, Catholics and most Protestants speak of original sin: every person is born sharing in Adam's fallen state, even in some sense his guilt. Orthodox Christians usually speak of ancestral sin: we inherit mortality and a wounded nature, but not Adam's personal guilt. Part of that difference goes back to how one small phrase in this passage was translated into Latin. What every church agrees on is Paul's direction of travel. The chapter doesn't end with Adam. It ends with grace reigning, through Jesus Christ.
screen: `BY ONE MAN SIN ENTERED.` · `BY THE OBEDIENCE OF ONE.` · `NOT AN EVEN SEESAW: MUCH MORE.` · `ORIGINAL SIN, ANCESTRAL SIN.` · then, large: `GRACE DID MUCH MORE ABOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice grace bigger than a mistake. Settle, and breathe. Think of a mistake, yours or someone else's, that turned out to be smaller than what came after it. A fight that ended in a better friendship. A wrong turn that led somewhere good. Someone who forgave you more than you expected. Don't explain it away. Just let yourself see that the mistake didn't get the last word. Breathe out, and let that sink in. If you pray, you can thank God for that grace, by name. The bell holds the time.
Adam and Christ. The first man and the one who obeyed, set side by side by Paul, with grace always the heavier side.
Your line: grace abounds. Today, when a mistake, yours or someone else's, looks like it's going to have the last word, say those two words under your breath. Day three hundred seventeen.

what it means: Paul sets them side by side: one opened the door to sin and death, one to life, and grace is always the heavier side.
what a scholar hears: Paul's Greek eph' hō in 5:12 likely means because all sinned, but the Latin Bible read in whom all sinned, which shaped Augustine's teaching on original sin.

318.title: Dead to sin (Romans 6)
318.hook: baptism as burial and rising: walk in newness of life
318.howItsDone: Romans 6:3–11 is read at many baptisms and at the Easter Vigil, and some Christians touch water on entering church, or recall their baptism each morning, as a reminder of dying and rising with Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adam and Christ on Paul's seesaw, and your line was grace abounds. Did a mistake try to have the last word, and did you answer it? Day three hundred eighteen.

Imagine a kid who's just been told: whatever you break, it's already forgiven. For about ten seconds the kid looks thoughtful. Then the kid looks at the china cabinet. Paul saw this coming. He's just said that where sin abounded, grace did much more abound, and he can hear someone in the back of the room raising a hand. Wait. If more sin means more grace, shouldn't we sin more? Give grace something to do? It's a sharp question, and maybe some people in Rome were really asking it. Paul answers with two words, and then with a picture of water, a grave and a morning. That picture is today.
screen: `WHATEVER YOU BREAK IS FORGIVEN.` → `SO SHOULD WE SIN MORE?` → `WATER, A GRAVE, A MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the question, in the King James Bible: "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." In Greek, me genoito: absolutely not, may it never be. Then Paul reaches for baptism. The Greek word baptizo means to dip, to plunge under. And Paul says going under the water is like going into a grave. "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." So the old life, the one run by sin, has been buried. You don't go back to the grave to live there. You walk out into a new morning. That's what dead to sin means for Paul: not that temptation disappears, but that it no longer owns you. He talks about slavery, a picture everyone in Rome knew all too well: you used to belong to one master, now you belong to another. And he ends the chapter with a line many Christians know by heart: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." Wages are earned. A gift is not. Churches practice baptism in different ways, so here's who says what. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and many Protestants baptize babies as well as adults, trusting God's grace comes first. Baptists and many others baptize only those old enough to confess faith themselves. Some pour water, some plunge the whole body under, and the Orthodox immerse even infants three times. But almost every church reads this chapter at baptisms, because the picture is the same: down into the water, up into new life.
screen: `SHALL WE CONTINUE IN SIN? GOD FORBID.` · `BAPTIZO: PLUNGED UNDER.` · `BURIED WITH HIM, RAISED TO WALK.` · `WAGES EARNED, A GIFT GIVEN.` · then, large: `WALK IN NEWNESS OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start one new habit. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing that belongs to an old way of living you'd like to leave behind. Scrolling the minute you wake up. A sharp tone with someone at home. Picture it going under, like the water in Paul's picture. Then picture what you'd do instead, one small, new thing, and see yourself doing it tomorrow morning. Make it tiny enough to actually start. If you pray, you can ask for help to walk in it. The bell holds the time.
Dead to sin. Paul's picture of baptism: the old life buried under the water, so it no longer owns you, and a new life walking out.
Your line: newness of life. Today, the next time you wash your hands or your face, let the water remind you of the one new habit you've chosen, and do it once. Day three hundred eighteen.

319.title: The wretched man (Romans 7:14–25)
319.hook: the good I want, I don't do
319.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 7 when talking honestly about habits and temptation, in confession, in recovery groups and in spiritual direction, where the struggle is named without shame.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dead to sin, baptism as a burial and a rising, and your line was newness of life. Did you try your one new habit? If it wobbled already, today is for you. Day three hundred nineteen.

It's eleven at night. You promised yourself you'd be in bed by ten. You know exactly why you should put the phone down. You want to put the phone down. And your thumb keeps scrolling, as if it belongs to someone else. Or it's the sharp word you swore you wouldn't say, and there it is, out of your mouth again. Everybody knows this feeling: wanting one thing and doing another. What's surprising is to find it in the middle of a letter by one of the most driven people in history. Right after Paul's big picture of new life, he writes the most honest paragraph in the whole letter.
screen: `ELEVEN AT NIGHT, STILL SCROLLING.` → `WANTING ONE THING, DOING ANOTHER.` → `PAUL'S MOST HONEST PARAGRAPH.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." Read it twice and you'll hear yourself. Paul says he agrees with God's law. He delights in it. He knows it's good. And still, something in him pulls the other way, like a second law at war inside him. The knowing isn't the problem. The doing is. Then the paragraph breaks open into a cry: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Wretched, in Greek talaiporos, means worn down, miserable, like someone exhausted by a long hardship. It isn't a pose. It's a groan. And notice the question he asks. Not how do I fix myself, but who shall deliver me? He's looking outside himself. And the answer comes in the very next breath: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." Now here's a real puzzle, and Christians have argued over it for sixteen centuries: who is this I? Some readers, including Augustine in his later years and Martin Luther, hear Paul describing the Christian life: even the baptized still feel this war inside, every day. Many early Greek teachers, and many scholars today, hear Paul speaking about life under the law without the Spirit, the way things look before chapter eight. The text doesn't settle it for us. But almost every reader recognizes the feeling. Paul's letter doesn't hide the struggle or scold it. It names it, and it cries out for help.
screen: `THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.` · `TWO LAWS AT WAR INSIDE.` · `WHO SHALL DELIVER ME?` · `WHO IS THIS I?` · then, large: `O WRETCHED MAN THAT I AM!`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with your own struggle. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing you keep doing that you don't want to do. Something small and real. Instead of the usual lecture you give yourself, try speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend who told you the same thing. Tired. Honest. Still trying. Notice where the struggle sits in your body, and let your breath go there. If you pray, you can say Paul's own question, who shall deliver me, and just wait with it. The bell holds the time.
The wretched man. Paul's cry, talaiporos in Greek: worn down by the war between the good he wants and what he does.

Your line: who shall deliver me? Today, when you catch yourself doing the thing you didn't want to do, skip the lecture. Take one breath, and ask for help, from God or from a friend. Day three hundred nineteen.
